content: The interventions described in the text focus on maternal mental health, child development, and parenting skills through various structured programs and strategies. 1. Community Health Worker (CHW) Home Visits: CHWs systematically visited every home in their assigned neighborhoods to identify pregnant mothers. They carried scales to weigh infants, plotted the weights on growth charts to identify underweight children, and recorded outcomes on government-issued Road-to-Health cards. Antenatal Messages: These included education on good maternal nutrition, preparation for breastfeeding, regular antenatal clinic attendance, recognition of danger signs, HIV testing, prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) tasks, partner prevention strategies, and cessation of alcohol use. Postnatal Messages: These focused on breastfeeding, growth monitoring, medical adherence (e.g., immunizations and HIV prevention for exposed children), infant bonding, and securing child grants. Monitoring: Home visits were monitored through handwritten notes and mobile phones that recorded visit details, including time, length, content covered, and perceived impact. 2. Mother and Baby Group Sessions: These group sessions combined education on child development with teaching and practicing age-appropriate play activities and toy-making to enhance development across all areas. The sessions were interactive and flexible, incorporating mothers' experiences at home. Discussions included setting limits, teaching good behavior, and addressing the costs and benefits of physical punishment, which had increased under the stress of internally displaced person (IDP) life. A final session focused on sustaining the knowledge gained and promoting mother-to-mother transmission of information. Home visits by psychosocial facilitators and nutrition support workers reinforced the knowledge shared in the group sessions and addressed specific behavioral or relational challenges. 3. Learning Through Play Program: Starting in the last trimester of pregnancy, this program provided center-based parent groups and fortnightly individual home visits. A pictorial calendar was used to depict eight stages of child development from birth to three years, with illustrations of parent-child play and activities promoting learning and attachment. The program emphasized the quality of mother-infant interaction, helping mothers read infant cues and develop sensitive responsiveness through play. Training materials were adapted to the local cultural context, with illustrations recreated by local artists to reflect cultural details. 4. Psychoeducation on Attachment Behaviors: Clinical psychologists provided mothers with detailed information on attachment behaviors during pregnancy. These included activities such as talking to the fetus, touching the mother’s abdomen to feel fetal movements, singing to the fetus, imagining breastfeeding, and paying attention to fetal movements. Fathers were encouraged to support and interact with the mother and fetus. Mothers were educated on the benefits of breastfeeding and the positive outcomes of talking to infants. Sessions included time for mothers to ask questions, and they were provided with instructional materials and a CD-ROM on mother-infant attachment behaviors. 5. Interactive and Supportive Education: Nurses delivered interactive, motivating, and supportive education sessions lasting 10-15 minutes during one-on-one bedside interactions. Techniques such as clarification, discussions, and the use of posters were employed. Mothers received a brochure with appealing photographs and clear, easy-to-understand content. Postnatal follow-up telephone support was provided within two weeks of discharge to reinforce knowledge and explore signs of cord infection. 6. Cognitive Behavioral and Interpersonal Interventions: Parents participated in active and interactive activities such as role-play, games, parent-child interactions, and group-based problem-solving. Parents were assigned homework to practice new skills with their child, spouse, or peers. Sessions included the use of colored posters to convey messages, and families received activity booklets with smaller versions of the posters. The program included introductory and concluding sessions, six sessions on child care, and four sessions on mother care, with one or two home visits to review parenting messages and address barriers to implementation. 7. Exercise and Emotional Self-Management: Programs included supervised physical exercise during pregnancy to reduce antenatal depression and emotional self-management training to prevent postnatal depression. These interventions were tailored to the cultural and individual needs of participants, with a focus on improving maternal mental health and overall well-being. 8. Nutrition and Psychosocial Support: Standard nutritional education and monitoring were combined with discussions to reinforce psychosocial knowledge and address specific challenges. Facilitators worked with mothers to promote aspects of child development according to individual needs and the home context. 9. Behavioral and Cognitive Skills Training: Interventions included problem-solving, emotional regulation, relaxation techniques, communication skills, and cognitive restructuring. Parents were taught to identify thoughts, monitor mood, and improve parent-child interactions. Social support and assertiveness training were also provided to enhance coping mechanisms. 10. Engagement and Social Support: Interventions emphasized active listening, empathy, collaboration, and involving spouses and family members. Mothers were encouraged to discuss the advantages of treatment, identify barriers, and commit to implementing learned practices. Case management and normalization of experiences were also key components. These interventions collectively aimed to improve maternal mental health, enhance parenting skills, and promote child development through structured, culturally sensitive, and evidence-based approaches.
